newsitem.title: USA: GM estimates strike costs at $225 million.
newsitem.headline: GM estimates strike costs at $225 million.

text.p: General Motors Corp. said Friday that ongoing strikes at plants in Oklahoma City and Pontiac, Mich., have cost the automaker about $225 million.

In its quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, GM said the assembly plant strikes have resulted in the loss of 54,000 vehicles as of Thursday. The lost profits are equal to 31 cents a share of GM common stock.
GM said in the filing that the estimated costs do not consider the effect of any vehicle recoveries that may result from production increases that the company is likely to pursue in future periods.
"The extent of such recoveries may be substantial depending on the timeliness of the resolutions of these work stoppages," GM said in the filing.
The Oklahoma City strike, which began April 4, has held back the launch of two important new mid-size sedans, the Chevrolet Malibu and the Oldsmobile Cutlass.
The Pontiac plant, which was halted by a strike on April 22, is one of three plants that produce GM's popular full-size Chevrolet and GMC full-size pickup trucks.

GM North American Operations President G. Richard Wagoner said on Wednesday he could not predict when the disputes will be resolved. In both strikes, the United Auto Workers has demanded that GM hire hundreds of new workers to cope with production line increases and to replace workers who retired.

Chrysler Corp estimated on Tuesday that a month-long strike at its Mound Road engine plant in Detroit, which forced it to shut down six truck assembly plants, will reduce the company's second quarter net income by $450 million, or 65 cents a share.
GM also this week settled a 24-hour strike by electrical components workers in Warren, Ohio, that had threatened a broader shutdown of its North American operations.
About 8,200 members of International Union of Electronic Workers Local 717 are scheduled to vote on the tentative agreement on May 23 and 24. The pact offers improved job security for workers.
